title: Setting up house — the me- prefix, part 1
goal: Meet the prefix that turns up in nearly every written Indonesian sentence. Learn how *me-* becomes *mem-*, *men-* or *meng-*, why *pakai* turns into *memakai*, and where the prefix vanishes in conversation.
bekal: build standard active verbs with *mem-*, *men-* and *meng-*: *membeli, mencari, mengantar*
drop the first sound of roots in *p*, *t* and *k*: *pakai → memakai, tulis → menulis, kirim → mengirim*
know when *me-* must disappear: *Tolong buka*, *Alamatnya saya kirim*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Di toko mebel
dialogs.intro: The following Saturday. The *kontrakan* came with a bed, a wardrobe and nothing else, so Mas Bayu, Sarah's new colleague, has taken her on his motorbike to a furniture shop on Jalan Parangtritis.

lines.text: Setuju. Saya bisa membayar lewat transfer, Pak?

lines.speaker: Bayu:
lines.text: Wah, baru seminggu di Yogya, Mbak Sarah sudah pintar menawar!

lines.literal: wah, new one-week at Yogya, Miss Sarah already clever bargain!

notes: **Membeli, mencari, membayar, menawar** — four verbs, four versions of one prefix. The roots are *beli, cari, bayar, tawar*; *me-* plus a nasal sound turns each into a standard active verb. The pattern behind the changes is in the grammar boxes below.

**Jangan langsung membayar.** The first price in a shop like this is an opening move. Furniture, market goods, *becak* rides and souvenirs are bargained over; supermarkets, cafés and anything with a printed price tag are not. Notice that *menawar* comes from *tawar* and ⚠️ the *t* has vanished.

**Kayu jati** is teak, the prestige wood of Java. Jepara, on Central Java's north coast, is famous for carved teak furniture. *Mebel* (from Dutch *meubel*) is the word on shop signs; *perabot* is the broader word for household things.

**Waduh** is "oh dear" or "ouch", said when something is a problem. A seller's *waduh* at your offer is part of the theatre, not real distress. *Belum bisa* ("can't yet") is the soft way to refuse: it leaves the door open for your next offer.

**Ongkos kirim**, shortened to *ongkir*, is the delivery charge; online shoppers talk about *gratis ongkir* (free delivery) all the time. *Dua juta pas* is exactly two million: *pas* means "exact, just right", as in *uang pas* (the exact money).

**Alamatnya nanti saya kirim** — here Sarah does **not** say *mengirim*, and she is right. When the object comes first and the doer is *saya*, the verb must be the bare root. That construction is the star of Unit 4; for now, just notice the missing prefix.

grammars.title: The me- prefix: mem-, men-, meng-
body: *Me-* makes an active verb from a root, and standard Indonesian uses it for almost every verb that takes an object. Its ending changes to match the first sound of the root, so that the two meet comfortably in the mouth.
after: Say them aloud and you will feel the logic: *m* is made with the lips, like *b* and *p*; *n* with the tongue behind the teeth, like *d* and *t*; *ng* at the back of the mouth, like *g* and *k*.

Not every verb takes *me-*. Verbs with *ber-* (*belajar, bekerja*) belong to another family, and many everyday verbs have no prefix at all: *makan, minum, pergi, tidur, datang*. A good dictionary shows which is which.

grammars.title: The sound that drops: p, t, k
body: When the root begins with *p*, *t* or *k*, that first sound is swallowed by the nasal. (So is *s*, which is Unit 3.) This is the one rule of the prefix that really needs practice.
after: ⚠️ The sound drops only when a vowel follows it. Loanwords that begin with two consonants keep them: *mentransfer*, *memproduksi*, *mengkritik*. A few famous words wobble even among editors: *mempengaruhi* is everywhere, though the dictionary prefers *memengaruhi*.
💬 In conversation the prefix is often left off altogether: *Saya cari meja*, *Kamu mau beli apa?* That is not a mistake, just speech. Writing, and careful speech, put it back.

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Dimas membantu
dialogs.intro: Sunday morning. The pick-up truck has barely left when Dimas, Bu Endang's ten-year-old grandson, appears at Sarah's door.

lines.text: Wah, bahasanya baku sekali! Tapi kamu belum mengangkat bukunya, lho.

notes: **Aku bantu, ya!** Dimas uses *aku*, as children do with almost everyone, and drops the prefix: *bantu* instead of *membantu*. An offer ending in *…, ya!* is less a question than an announcement.

**Tolong buka** — requests and commands always take the bare root: *Tolong buka*, never *Tolong membuka*. The same goes for *Buka!*, *Coba lihat*, *Ayo makan*. It is one of the places where *me-* must disappear, even in writing.

**Siap!**, literally "ready!", comes from military drill and now means "yes, boss" or "on it". **Beres** is "sorted, done, no problem". Both are cheerful and casual, and colleagues use them as much as children do.

**Jangan sampai jatuh** — *jangan sampai* means "make sure it doesn't…", a warning about an outcome rather than an order: *Jangan sampai terlambat* (mind you're not late). Plain *Jangan jatuh!* would sound like a command to the books.

**PR** (said *pé-ER*) is *pekerjaan rumah*, homework, literally "house work". Indonesian schoolchildren write their *cerita* (stories, compositions) in careful standard Indonesian, which is why Dimas suddenly sounds like a newsreader.

**Nulis, ngangkat** — the prefix squashed into a single nasal sound, like Rina's *nunggu* in Unit 1: standard *menulis, mengangkat*, spoken *nulis, ngangkat*. Unit 3 gives you the full set of these spoken forms.

grammars.title: Said or written: where me- disappears
body: The prefix belongs to standard Indonesian. In two places it must go even in writing; in relaxed speech it goes almost everywhere.
after: The first two rows are grammar: getting them wrong sounds foreign, and *Tolong membuka* is a classic learner's slip. The last three are register: choose according to who you are talking to.
⚠️ *Jangan* can go either way. You say *Jangan pegang!* to a child; a printed sign says *Jangan membuang sampah di sini* (do not throw rubbish here).
Dimas shows the whole system in two lines: *Aku bantu* when he talks, *Saya membantu* when he writes his homework. Most Indonesians switch like this many times a day without noticing.

blocks.text: Most *kontrakan* come empty or nearly so. These are the words you will need at the *toko mebel* and the market.
The *guling* deserves a word: a long bolster that Indonesians hug while they sleep, and which every bed has. Foreigners laugh at it, then buy one, then never go back.

blocks.title: Bargaining in five lines
items: *Harga pasnya berapa?* — What's your real price?
*Kalau ambil dua, berapa?* — And if I take two?
*Ya sudah, segitu saja.* — Fine, that much then.
*Nggak jadi, deh. Terima kasih.* — I'll leave it, thanks. (Walking away politely is often the best offer you can make.)

blocks.text: A dictionary lists *memilih* under *pilih*, so to look a word up you must undo the prefix in your head. Most cases are easy; one is ambiguous.

The last row is the tricky one: *mengirim* comes from *kirim*, but *mengantar* comes from *antar*. When in doubt, look under both. The remaining forms, *meny-*, *menge-* and plain *me-*, arrive in Unit 3.
Cover the Indonesian column, read the English, and rebuild each sentence from memory.
